families.title: Footprint borders
families.mathematics: A border is one cell of footprints repeated forever along a strip, each footprint a notched F in one of four forms: as drawn, flipped across, flipped down and half-turned. A move of the copy that keeps the strip on itself is a slide, the flip over the middle line, a glide (the flip and a slide), a flip across a line straight across the strip, or a half-turn round a point of the middle line, and it matches when every F lands on an F of the form the move makes it. Since the F has no symmetry, where one F lands decides a move, so one F that lands on a gap or a different F rules a move out, and one F whose turned or flipped-across form a row never has rules out every half-turn or every flip across at once. A border has Fs in both rows, so every symmetry keeps the middle line and these moves are all of them. A glide done twice is a slide, so when the flip alone fails the shortest glide is half the shortest slide; two flips over perpendicular lines make the half-turn round their crossing. These are the moves of frieze groups, which come in seven kinds.
rules: The border repeats its cell forever both ways. Only the Fs count, not the strip’s ends or the lines.
A border has Fs in both rows: while a row is empty, no claim can be made and nothing is solved.
A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.
A slide must move the copy. A glide is the flip over the middle line followed by a slide along it.
The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.

puzzles.title: Footprint borders playground
puzzles.objective: Make a border, and try every move of the copy on it.
puzzles.instruction: Make a border, and try every move of the copy on it.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. A glide is the flip over the middle line and then a slide. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The buttons below flip it over the middle line, flip it across or turn it halfway round, where it is. Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. The numbers set how many places the cell has.

puzzles.idea: Free play: build a border in a cell of 2 to 6 places and test slides, the flip, glides, flips across and half-turns.
puzzles.prerequisites: None. A grown-up can suggest what to try.
hints: Put one as-drawn F in the cell and slide the copy. Which slides match?
Add a flipped-down F straight below it, then flip the copy.
Move the flipped-down F one place along. Which moves match now?

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts which F the copy will show before pressing a button, and checks one F at a time.
parent.prompt: Which moves match this border, and which F tells you that one doesn’t?
parent.explanation: A move of the copy that keeps the strip on itself is a slide, the flip over the middle line, a glide (the flip and a slide), a flip across a line straight across the strip, or a half-turn round a point of the middle line. Since the F has no symmetry, one F decides each move: it must land on an F of the form the move makes it. The guide’s witnesses (p. 3) are good borders to build: T (slides only), G (a glide, no flip), H (the flip, no half-turn), R (half-turns, no flips) and E (both flips and the half-turn).
parent.extension: Make a border with every kind of move. How few Fs does it need?
parent.connection: There are seven kinds of frieze, by which of these moves match (Gallian, Ch. 28); the puzzles do not need the list.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 throughout, and K–1 Problem 7 (trade borders and find the moves that match).

puzzles.objective: Slide the copy along the border until it matches.

puzzles.idea: A slide matches only when every F lands on one facing the same way; here that first happens a whole cell along.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. No reading or counting.
hints: Watch the as-drawn F in the copy. Where is the next one like it in its row?
Slides of 1 or 2 places put that F on a gap or on a flipped-across F.
Slide the copy 3 places.

parent.notice: Whether your child watches one F (the as-drawn one, say) and slides until it reaches the next one like it, or slides until nothing is red.
parent.prompt: Which F tells you fastest that a slide misses?
parent.explanation: The F has no symmetry, so a matching slide must carry the as-drawn F in the top row onto another as-drawn F in the top row. The next one is 3 places along, and a 3-place slide carries every F onto its own repeat; slides of 1 or 2 places put it on the flipped-across F or a gap. A 3-place slide either way matches, and so does every multiple of 3.
parent.extension: Make a border where a 1-place slide matches. (The same F in every place of a row.)
parent.connection: The matching slides of a border are all the multiples of the shortest one, a subgroup of the translations (Gallian, Ch. 28).

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 K–1 Problem 1 (find slides that match and slides that do not), on a given border; the border is new.

puzzles.title: How far?
puzzles.objective: Find the shortest slide that matches, then press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F like it that shows why.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the shortest slide that matches.
puzzles.instruction: Find the shortest slide that matches, then press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F like it that shows why.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. Once the copy matches, press Shortest, then tap an F and the nearest F it could land on, as far as the copy went.

puzzles.idea: The cell drawn need not be the shortest repeat: the shortest slide is set by the nearest F like a given one.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. Compare two distances by eye.
hints: Find a slide that matches. How do you know no shorter slide does?
Every F must land on an F like it in its own row. How far is the nearest one like the as-drawn F?
Slide the copy 2 places, press Shortest, then tap an as-drawn F and the next one along.

parent.notice: Whether your child stops at the first match they see, 4 places along, where the copy’s frame lines up with the cell.
parent.prompt: The cell is 4 places long. Must the shortest slide be 4?
parent.explanation: The cell is 4 places, but the border repeats every 2: in the top row as-drawn and flipped-across Fs take turns, and a half-turned F sits below every other place. A slide must carry an as-drawn F onto another in its own row, and the nearest is 2 places away, so no shorter slide can match, and the 2-place slide carries every F onto one like it. That pair is the certificate. The 4-place slide matches too; claiming it is refused, because a nearer as-drawn F is 2 places away.
parent.extension: Draw the same border with a cell of 2 places. Is it the same border?
parent.connection: The guide’s warning: do not infer the shortest period from the block a child happened to draw. The matching slides are the multiples of the primitive period.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 K–1 Problem 2, grades 2–3 Problem 1 and grades 4–5 Problem 1 (shortest matching slides), with the guide’s warning that a drawn block need not be the shortest repeat (p. 4); the border is new.

puzzles.title: A glide
puzzles.objective: Make a border that matches after a glide, a flip and a slide, but not after the flip alone, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a border that matches after a glide but not after the flip alone.
puzzles.instruction: Make a border that matches after a glide, a flip and a slide, but not after the flip alone, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. A glide is the flip over the middle line and then a slide. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The button below flips it over the middle line where it is. Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. A crossed-out move must not match. Once the copy has tried it, press its Can’t, then tap an F and the place that move puts it, which has no F like it.

A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.
A slide must move the copy. A glide is the flip over the middle line followed by a slide along it.
The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: A glide can match when neither of its parts, the flip or the slide, matches alone.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. No reading: a grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Put an F in each row, then flip the copy and slide it.
After the flip, an F in the top row lands in the bottom row, flipped down. Put that F in the bottom row, but not straight below.
One answer: an as-drawn F in the top row, place 1, and a flipped-down F in the bottom row, place 2. Flip and slide 1, then press Can’t and tap the as-drawn F and the gap below it.

parent.notice: Whether your child builds a flip first (an F straight above its flipped-down twin) and then has to move one of the pair.
parent.prompt: After the flip, where does this F land? What would have to be there?
parent.explanation: After the flip, an F in the top row lands straight below itself, flipped down. For a glide to match, the bottom row must hold that flipped-down F some places along; for the flip alone to fail, some F must have a gap or a different F straight across the middle line. With a 2-place cell, 20 borders work, such as the guide’s Border G: an as-drawn F above and a flipped-down F below, one place along. The certificate for Can’t is one F and the place straight across from it.
parent.extension: Can a border match after the glide and after the flip? (Yes: put each flipped-down F straight below; then a flip and a slide of a whole cell is a glide.)
parent.connection: Gallian’s frieze pattern II (Ch. 28, pp. 446–449): a glide reflection with no reflection, whose square is the smallest translation.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 K–1 Problem 3 and grades 2–3 Problem 2 (a glide that works when the flip alone fails); the guide’s Border G is one answer.

puzzles.title: Move the Fs
puzzles.objective: Move Fs so that a glide matches but the flip alone doesn’t, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Move Fs so a glide matches but the flip alone doesn’t.
puzzles.instruction: Move Fs so that a glide matches but the flip alone doesn’t, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. A glide is the flip over the middle line and then a slide. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The button below flips it over the middle line where it is. Tap an F in the cell to pick it up, then tap an empty place to put it there. A crossed-out move must not match. Once the copy has tried it, press its Can’t, then tap an F and the place that move puts it, which has no F like it.

The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: Moving the bottom row half a cell along turns a flip border into a glide border: the old move breaks, the glide stays.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. No reading: a grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Flip the copy. Why does the flip alone match now?
The flipped-down F is straight below the as-drawn F. Move one of them a place along.
Move the as-drawn F to the top row, place 2. Flip and slide 1, then press Can’t.

parent.notice: Whether your child moves one F and tests again, or moves both and loses the glide.
parent.prompt: What has to be straight below the as-drawn F for the flip to match?
parent.explanation: The start is the guide’s Border H: the flip matches because the flipped-down F is straight below the as-drawn one. Moving either F one place along breaks the flip and keeps a glide: after the flip, the as-drawn F lands on a gap, and a flip with a 1-place slide carries it onto the flipped-down F. Exactly 4 arrangements work: the two Fs in different rows and different places.
parent.extension: Put it back with one move. Which move did each change break, and which did it keep?
parent.connection: The guide’s K–1 Problem 5 edit: shift the lower row of Border H half a period to get Border G.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 K–1 Problem 5 (make a flip border, then change it so the flip fails) and grades 2–3 Problem 6, starting from the guide’s Border H.

puzzles.title: A half-turn
puzzles.objective: Make a border that matches after a half-turn but not after the flip, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a border that matches after a half-turn but not after the flip.
puzzles.instruction: Make a border that matches after a half-turn but not after the flip, then press Can’t and show why the flip fails.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The buttons below flip it over the middle line or turn it halfway round, where it is. Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. A crossed-out move must not match. Once the copy has tried it, press its Can’t, then tap an F and the place that move puts it, which has no F like it.

The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: A half-turn carries each F to the other row, half-turned, so it needs different partners from the flip.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. No reading: a grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Put an F in each row, then turn the copy and slide the turned copy along.
Turned halfway, an F in the top row lands in the bottom row as a half-turned F.
One answer: an as-drawn F in the top row, place 1, and a half-turned F in the bottom row, place 2. Turn, try the flip alone, then press Can’t.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects the flip and the half-turn to need the same thing below, and what they see when the flip misses.
parent.prompt: Turned halfway, which F does the as-drawn F become, and in which row?
parent.explanation: A half-turn round a point of the middle line carries an F to the other row, half-turned, as far on the other side of the point. So the bottom row must hold the half-turned F of each F above (and the reverse), while the flip needs the flipped-down one straight below. The guide’s Border R, an as-drawn F above and a half-turned F below one place along, has the half-turn round the point midway between them and no flip. With a 2-place cell, 40 borders work.
parent.extension: Find every point a half-turn of your border goes round. (For Border R, one every place along the middle line, here; half a cell apart.)
parent.connection: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 5; the half-turn centres of Border R are spaced half a period apart (guide p. 3).

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 2–3 Problem 5, K–1 Problem 6 and grades 4–5 Problem 5 (a half-turn that matches when the flip fails); the guide’s Border R is one answer.

puzzles.title: Flip, no turn
puzzles.objective: Make a border that matches after the flip but never after a half-turn, round any point of the middle line, then press Can’t and show an F a half-turn can’t place.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a border that matches after the flip but never after a half-turn.
puzzles.instruction: Make a border that matches after the flip but never after a half-turn, round any point of the middle line, then press Can’t and show an F a half-turn can’t place.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The buttons below flip it over the middle line or turn it halfway round, where it is. Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. A crossed-out half-turn or flip across must fail everywhere. Once the copy has tried it, press its Can’t, tap an F, then the F it would become.
rules: The border repeats its cell forever both ways. Only the Fs count, not the strip’s ends or the lines.
A border has Fs in both rows: while a row is empty, no claim can be made and nothing is solved.
A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.
A slide must move the copy. A glide is the flip over the middle line followed by a slide along it.
The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: One F whose half-turned form the other row never has rules out a half-turn round every point of the middle line at once.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. No reading: a grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Make a border that matches after the flip first, then try turning the copy at a few places.
Turned halfway, an as-drawn F becomes a half-turned F in the other row. Can you keep every half-turned F out of that row?
One answer: an as-drawn F in the top row, place 1, and a flipped-down F below it. Turn the copy, then press Can’t, tap the as-drawn F, then the half-turned F.

parent.notice: Whether your child tests the turn round one or two points and stops, or looks for a reason that covers every point of the middle line.
parent.prompt: Wherever on the middle line the turn goes round, which F would this one have to land on?
parent.explanation: A half-turn round any point of the middle line carries an F to the other row, half-turned. So if the other row never holds the half-turned form of some F, no half-turn round any point of the middle line can match: that F has nowhere to land. The guide’s Border H, an as-drawn F above a flipped-down one, has the flip and no half-turn: a turned as-drawn F needs a half-turned F in the bottom row, and there is none. One F and the form it turns into are the certificate. With a 2-place cell, 20 borders work, and every one has such an F.
parent.extension: Can a border have the flip and the flip across, but no half-turn? (No: the two flips make a half-turn; see puzzle 10.)
parent.connection: Week 35 grades 2–3 Problem 4, and the guide’s note that failure round one chosen centre does not rule out every half-turn.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 2–3 Problem 4 and K–1 Problem 6 (no half-turn round any point; here, any point of the middle line, with Fs in both rows); the guide’s Border H is one answer.

puzzles.title: Slide and glide
puzzles.objective: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide that match. For each, press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F of the form it needs.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide.
puzzles.instruction: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide that match. For each, press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F of the form it needs.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. A glide is the flip over the middle line and then a slide. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The button below flips it over the middle line where it is. Once the copy matches, press Shortest, then tap an F and the nearest F it could land on, as far as the copy went.

A border has Fs in both rows: while a row is empty, no claim can be made and nothing is solved.
A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.

The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: A glide done twice is a slide, so when the flip alone fails the shortest glide is half the shortest slide.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. Compare distances by eye.
hints: Find a slide that matches, then a glide. Which F has the nearest F like it in its row?
After the flip, the as-drawn F must land on a flipped-down F in the bottom row. How far is the nearest one?
Slide 4 and tap the as-drawn F and the next one; then flip, slide 2, and tap the as-drawn F and the flipped-down F 2 places along.

parent.notice: Whether your child compares the glide with the slide, and guesses the glide from the slide before sliding the flipped copy.
parent.prompt: What happens if you do the glide twice?
parent.explanation: The cell repeats every 4 places and no shorter slide matches: the as-drawn F has no other as-drawn F nearer than 4 places in its row. Flipped, that F needs a flipped-down F in the bottom row, and the nearest is 2 places along; the 2-place glide carries every F onto one like it. The glide done twice is the 4-place slide. In general, when the flip alone fails, the shortest glide is exactly half the shortest slide.
parent.extension: Could a border have a shortest glide of 3 and a shortest slide of 4? (No: two 3-place glides make a 6-place slide, and 6 is not a multiple of 4.)
parent.connection: The guide’s shortest glide theorem (p. 6): every glide displacement is (k + ½)P when the bare flip fails; Gallian’s pattern II.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 2 (shortest slide and shortest glide) and grades 2–3 Problem 3 (compare them); the border is new.

puzzles.title: Turn only
puzzles.objective: Make a border that matches after a half-turn, but not after the flip over the middle line or a flip across anywhere, then show why each flip fails.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a border with a half-turn but no flip over the middle or across.

Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. A crossed-out move must not match. puzzles.idea: A flip across keeps an F in its row, flipped across; one F whose flipped-across form its row lacks rules out every such line at once.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. A grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Make a border that matches after a half-turn first, then try both flips.
Flipped across, an F stays in its row as its flipped-across form. Keep that form out of its row.
One answer: an as-drawn F in the top row, place 1, and a half-turned F in the bottom row, place 2.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries Flip across at a few places and then looks for one reason that covers them all.
parent.prompt: Wherever the line goes, what would this F become, and is there one in its row?
parent.explanation: The flip needs each F’s flipped-down form straight across the middle line; a flip across any line straight across the strip keeps each F in its row, flipped across; a half-turn needs it in the other row, half-turned. The guide’s Border R (an as-drawn F above and a half-turned F below, one place along) has the half-turn and neither flip: the as-drawn F has a gap straight below it, and its row has no flipped-across F at all, which rules out every line across at once. With a 2-place cell, 36 borders work.
parent.extension: Change one F so that the half-turn fails but both flips still fail.
parent.connection: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 5 and the guide: at an upper as-drawn F, either kind of flip needs a missing mirror form, which rules out every perpendicular axis, not only the one through a displayed centre.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 5 (a half-turn, no flip over the middle line, no flip across a perpendicular line); the guide’s Border R is one answer.

The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: Breaking a slide changes the glide too: a glide done twice is a slide, so with a 4-place repeat the glide must be 2 places.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. Count up to 4 places. A grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Slide the copy 2 places, then flip it and slide it. Which moves match now?
To break the 2-place slide, the two as-drawn Fs must not be 2 places apart. Where must the flipped-down Fs go then?
One answer: as-drawn Fs in the top row, places 1 and 2, and flipped-down Fs in the bottom row, places 3 and 4.

parent.notice: Whether your child breaks the slide first, finds the glide broken too, and moves the flipped-down Fs to bring it back.
parent.prompt: If the glide goes 2 places, where must the flipped-down F for this as-drawn F be?
parent.explanation: The start is the guide’s Border G drawn with a 4-place cell: it repeats every 2 places, so the 2-place slide matches, and so does a 1-place glide. To break the 2-place slide, the four Fs must stop repeating every 2 places while the cell still repeats every 4. A glide done twice is a slide, so the glide must now be 2 places (twice 2 is 4); a 1-place glide would bring back the 2-place slide. For example, as-drawn Fs at places 1 and 2 above and flipped-down Fs at places 3 and 4 below. 20 arrangements work. The certificate for the slide is one F and the place 2 along where it lands.
parent.extension: Can you break the 2-place slide but keep a 1-place glide? (No: two 1-place glides make the 2-place slide.)
parent.connection: Week 35 grades 2–3 Problem 6, using its “larger repeating part”; the guide’s edit of Border T breaks an old slide the same way.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 2–3 Problem 6 (move footprints so an old matching move fails but the border still repeats, with a larger repeating part), starting from the guide’s Border G in a doubled cell.

puzzles.title: Two crossing flips
puzzles.objective: Make a border that matches after the flip over the middle line and after the flip across the crossing line, then tap the point a half-turn goes round.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make both flips match, then show where a half-turn goes round.
puzzles.instruction: Make a border that matches after the flip over the middle line and after the flip across the crossing line, then tap the point a half-turn goes round.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The buttons below flip it over the middle line or flip it across, where it is. Choose an F below, then tap a place to put it there; tap it again to take it away. Then press Turn here and tap the point a half-turn goes round.
rules: The border repeats its cell forever both ways. Only the Fs count, not the strip’s ends or the lines.
A border has Fs in both rows: while a row is empty, no claim can be made and nothing is solved.
A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.
A slide must move the copy. A glide is the flip over the middle line followed by a slide along it.
The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: Two flips over lines crossing at right angles make the half-turn round the crossing: one flip and then the other turns the copy halfway, so a border with both flips has that half-turn.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. Picture two flips one after the other. A grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Make a border that matches after the flip over the middle line first.
Flipped across the crossing line, each F lands in its row, flipped across, as far on the other side. Build the Fs in fours.
One answer: in the top row a flipped-across F in place 2 and an as-drawn F in place 3, and below them a half-turned F and a flipped-down F. Then tap where the two lines cross.

parent.notice: Whether your child taps the crossing straight away, presses both flips to see the copy turned, or looks among the dots for another point a turned copy fits.
parent.prompt: Flip this F over the middle line, then across the crossing line. Where does it end up, and which way is it facing?
parent.explanation: The flip over the middle line takes (x, y) to (x, −y), and the flip across the crossing line takes (x, y) to (−x, y), measuring from the crossing. One after the other they take (x, y) to (−x, −y): the half-turn round the crossing. So any border with both flips matches after that half-turn; pressing one flip and then the other turns the copy halfway and shows it. Every answer has its Fs in fours like the guide’s Border E: an F, its flipped-across twin opposite the crossing line, and both flipped down below. Other centres work too, one every half of the shortest slide along the middle line, because a half-turn followed by a slide is another half-turn.
parent.extension: Which other points does a half-turn go round? (Here, every 2 places along from the crossing; every place for a border that repeats every 2.)
parent.connection: Reflections in two perpendicular lines compose to the half-turn about their crossing; Gallian’s pattern VII has both reflections and hence the half-turns.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 4 (flips over two crossing lines, and the motions they force), with its printed crossing line; the guide’s Border E is the model.

puzzles.title: A longer border
puzzles.objective: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide that match. For each, press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F of the form it needs.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide.
puzzles.instruction: Find the shortest slide and the shortest glide that match. For each, press Shortest and tap an F and the nearest F of the form it needs.
puzzles.controls: A border repeats its framed cell forever both ways. The blue copy matches when every F in it lands on an F facing exactly the same way. A glide is the flip over the middle line and then a slide. Drag the copy to slide it, or use the arrow keys. The button below flips it over the middle line where it is. Once the copy matches, press Shortest, then tap an F and the nearest F it could land on, as far as the copy went.
rules: The border repeats its cell forever both ways. Only the Fs count, not the strip’s ends or the lines.
A border has Fs in both rows: while a row is empty, no claim can be made and nothing is solved.
A match needs every F of the copy on an F facing the same way.
A slide must move the copy. A glide is the flip over the middle line followed by a slide along it.
The copy stays on the strip: a half-turn goes round a point of the middle line, and a flip across goes over a line straight across the strip.
puzzles.idea: Two Fs alike and close together don’t make a short slide: the F with no near twin decides it.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell the four Fs apart by the notch and the arrow. Compare distances by eye.
hints: Find a slide and a glide that match. How do you know no shorter ones do?
Two as-drawn Fs in the top row are 2 places apart, but the 2-place slide misses. Which F has no F like it nearby?
The flipped-across F is alone in its row: the next is 6 places along. Flipped, it needs a half-turned F in the bottom row, and the nearest is 3 places along.

parent.notice: Whether your child claims a 2-place slide from the two as-drawn Fs, and then looks for the F that breaks it.
parent.prompt: Which F is alone in its row?
parent.explanation: The two as-drawn Fs in the top row are 2 places apart, but the 2-place slide carries the second onto the flipped-across F, so it misses; the border repeats only every 6 places. The flipped-across F shows it: it is the only one in its row, and the next is 6 places along. Flipped, that F needs a half-turned F in the bottom row, and the nearest is 3 places along; the 3-place glide matches, half of 6. The as-drawn Fs can’t certify either answer: each has another as-drawn F 2 places away, and a flipped-down F 1 place away.
parent.extension: Change two Fs so the border repeats every 2 places. Which glide matches then? (Make the top row all as-drawn and the bottom all flipped-down: a 1-place glide.)
parent.connection: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problem 1: explain why a smaller slide cannot match, by tracking one F whose nearest twin is far away.

puzzles.provenance: Week 35 grades 4–5 Problems 1 and 2 (why no smaller slide matches; shortest slide and glide); the border is new.
